newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rapeseed crop needs rain, southwest at risk.
newsitem.headline: French rapeseed crop needs rain, southwest at risk.

text.p: A three-month dry spell is raising fears of drought in France but with the exception of the southwest there is no reason to worry about the fate of the rapeseed crop if it rains in the coming weeks, a crop expert said on Monday.
Warm temperatures since March have helped up speed up plant development and the crop is now in full bloom, some 15 days ahead of schedule.
"The potential for the rapeseed crop has been hit only on the light soils of the southwest," an analyst from the French oilseeds research institute Cetiom said.
He predicted a maximum average yield for the region of two tonnes per hectare, down from a previous estimate of three tonne, if there is a break in the weather over the next few weeks.
But he cautioned that rapeseed sowings in the southwest were a marginal 100,000 hectares.
Last week the farm ministry forecast spring and winter rapeseed sowings for the 1997 harvest at 947,000 hectares, up 8.2 percent over 1996.
At this stage rain in late April or early May could still help reverse the situation in other regions, the analyst said.
"Rain could still allow for good yields," he said.
Sunflower sowings are still under way with 50 to 90 percent of area planted, depending on regions.
But moisture levels will be crucial to support above-ground growth between the second half of April and the first week of May.
Sunflowers sown in late March on a few patches are already above the ground, he said.
